author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Pleasure/suffering: see Buddhism

Personal identity: same, plus Parfit

Most ML theory: doesn't help scale deep learning

Planning: when did you last make a plan with 3+ steps? Abstraction does most of the work

Rationality: mostly just nudges intelligence in the right direction

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Fitness: is only defined locally, with respect to a population

GDP: same, GDP comparisons over time are very hacky

Welfare: you can't untangle selfish vs altruistic preferences

International law: see IR realism

The scientific method: *what* scientific method? See Strevens

For each group, exercising their own type of power seems ordinary and banal.

Being on the receiving end, though, is often unpredictable and overwhelming. Hence exercises of power propagate chilling effects (as people steer well clear of risk) which are hard for outsiders to see.

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @robbensinger I like "relations of ideas" exactly because it doesn't have this "eyes closed" implication! The most interesting relations are between ideas we've acquired via extensive observation - e.g. scientific theorising. Also "ideas" seems a better-grounded concept than "possible worlds".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @juliagalef @Meaningness @slatestarcodex @glenweyl Ofc claim 2 is true, but how do we know which heuristics will make our beliefs more accurate? author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex Just as, even though we know lightspeed limits are a universal constraint, they may only very tangentially affect the design of trains that operate within the boundaries of, say, a single solar system.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex I guess my intuition is that ideal Bayesian reasoners are sufficiently far from humans that you need to *start* with a wise justification for why we should expect epistemological principles derived from the former to be helpful for self-improvement by the latter.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@juliagalef @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex As discussed here, idk what counts as bayes-violating. https://t.co/akwzqK2Cpr

And how do we know there aren't many pragmatic principles which lead to less bayes-violating things, but are nevertheless so obviously dumb that we don't adopt them? I.e. is this post-hoc reasoning?

quoted.text: @juliagalef @Meaningness @slatestarcodex @glenweyl But this happens all the time - e.g. it's often a good idea to revise old beliefs even when you haven't received new evidence. (And see halfway down this post for a much longer list: https://t.co/hyBDq3Cntf)

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex E.g. consider the principle "never update except when you get new evidence". This is clearly dumb. But the link between this and Bayes is just as strong as it is for principles like "ensure your credences don't sum to more than 1".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex You've identified a bunch of principles which seem both bayes-endorsed, and also practically useful. But how do we distinguish *deriving* them from Bayes, vs finding post-hoc connections between them and Bayes?

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex I think I agree with all of this. Yet suppose we try to use knowledge of Bayes to improve our thinking - then we need to explicitly identify which thinking Bayes endorses or rejects in the context of human-level reasoning. But that involves accounting for the underlying mess.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex My intention for the analogy: the laws govern *ideal reasoning* but only weakly inform our attempts to design better human reasoning, like how relativity governs photons but only weakly informs train design (even though, in the limit, the best train will go as fast as a photon).

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex Yepp, this is the thing I'm pointing at. The explicit/verbal bit is important because that's how people can learn about which reasoning bayesianism disapproves of.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex I guess you'd say that you're constraining the power of the informal reasoning step, rather than the power of the inferences made when people cite this informal reasoning step? But in general I can't identify all the reasoning steps that contribute to reaching a given conclusion.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex Cool, thanks for clarifying. But for almost all practical arguments, I already have an overwhelming amount of relevant sensory evidence. author: RichardMCNgo
text: @ESYudkowsky @Meaningness @juliagalef @jonathanstray @alexeyguzey @othercriteria @glenweyl @slatestarcodex Oh, I agree relativity itself is very relevant to trains! author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @juliagalef @Meaningness @slatestarcodex @glenweyl I agree that using bayes as a guide is very reasonable! author: RichardMCNgo
text: @juliagalef @Meaningness @slatestarcodex @glenweyl I didn't ask how it constrains practical reasoning, but how it's relevant at all.  You say, as a guide. author: RichardMCNgo
text:
So my proposed six languages:

Libertarians talk about liberty-coercion and growth-dysfunction.

Conservatives talk about civilisation-barbarism and authority-subversion.

Progressives talk about oppressor-oppressed and equality-inequality.

Thoughts? Cc @EconTalker, @KlingBlog.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
According to Haidt's moral foundations theory, conservatives care more about authority, and sanctity, and loyalty. The first seems most distinctive and impactful.

Meanwhile progressives care a lot about equality even when there's no oppression, and equate fairness with equality.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Problem: the growth-dysfunction axis doesn't by itself justify disliking authoritarianism. But the liberty-coercion axis doesn't convey the pragmatic appeal of libertarianism. So maybe we should expand to two axes each - which also helps flesh out the other two perspectives.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The libertarian-leaning people I know most often justify their views along an axis which I'll call growth-dysfunction. I.e. if we implement libertarian policies, we'll make great economic and technological progress. If not, our societies will stagnate. Economists tend to agree.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
In "The Three Languages of Politics", Arnold Kling argues that progressives tend to frame issues in terms of an oppressor-oppressed axis; conservatives use a civilization-barbarism axis; and libertarians use a liberty-coercion axis.

But this seems incomplete. 1/5
